content: 1. The pH of a solution is calculated as the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration. Acidosis increases extracellular fluid (ECF) hydrogen ion concentration, thereby lowering the pH, while alkalosis decreases ECF hydrogen ion concentration, raising the pH. 2. Under normal physiological conditions, carbon dioxide (CO2) is produced in body tissues through intracellular metabolic processes, such as the oxidation of fats, carbohydrates, and amino acid carbon skeletons. This CO2 is then eliminated via the lungs, maintaining equilibrium. 3. CO2 generated in tissues diffuses into the blood due to the higher partial pressure of CO2 in tissues compared to the blood. This diffusion follows the principle of gases moving from areas of high pressure to low pressure. 4. The blood transports CO2 to the lungs, where it diffuses into the alveoli and is expelled into the atmosphere through pulmonary ventilation. 5. In red blood cells, CO2 reversibly combines with water under the influence of the enzyme carbonic anhydrase to form carbonic acid (H2CO3). This carbonic acid dissociates into hydrogen ions (H+) and bicarbonate ions (HCO3−). 6. Bicarbonate ions (HCO3−) diffuse out of red blood cells into the plasma, while chloride ions (Cl−) move into the red blood cells to maintain electrical neutrality. This process is known as the chloride shift. 7. Approximately 70% of CO2 from tissues is transported to the lungs as plasma bicarbonate ions. The remaining CO2 is transported as carbaminohemoglobin (23%) and dissolved CO2 in blood fluids (7%). 8. Respiratory alkalosis is almost always caused by increased alveolar respiration (hyperventilation), which reduces blood CO2 concentration, measured as PaCO2. This reduction in CO2 leads to decreased hydrogen ion and bicarbonate ion concentrations, resulting in an increase in pH and the development of alkalosis. 9. Compensation for respiratory alkalosis occurs through plasma buffers and proteins (e.g., hemoglobin in red blood cells and plasma proteins) in the acute stage and through renal mechanisms in the chronic compensatory stage. 10. In the acute compensatory stage, which begins within minutes to hours, the body’s non-bicarbonate buffers (e.g., hemoglobin, intracellular proteins, and phosphates) mediate the response. Cellular uptake of bicarbonate (HCO3−) occurs, and intracellular phosphates and proteins buffer the changes. For every 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO2, serum bicarbonate decreases by 1–2 mEq/L. The pH change is unpredictable. 11. In the chronic compensatory stage, renal mechanisms reduce tubular hydrogen ion (H+) secretion in response to decreased PaCO2. Within renal tubular cells, CO2 combines with water under the influence of carbonic anhydrase to form carbonic acid (H2CO3), which dissociates into bicarbonate (HCO3−) and hydrogen ions (H+). Alkalosis inhibits carbonic anhydrase activity, reducing H+ secretion into the renal tubule. Consequently, not all filtered bicarbonate reacts with H+ and is excreted in the urine, leading to reduced bicarbonate stores in the body. This process begins after 24–36 hours, with renal compensation completing within 36–72 hours. For every 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO2, serum bicarbonate decreases by 5 mEq/L, and pH approaches near-normal levels. 12. Respiratory alkalosis is classified into two types: acute and chronic. Acute respiratory alkalosis lasts less than 24–48 hours and is characterized by hyperventilation, which blows off excess CO2. Chronic respiratory alkalosis lasts longer than 24–48 hours, with metabolic compensation reducing the alkalosis effect of decreased blood CO2. 13. Common risk factors for respiratory alkalosis include advanced age, mechanical ventilation, lung diseases, hepatic failure, infections, high altitude, anxiety disorders, and central nervous system (CNS) infections. Less common risk factors include drug use and poisoning. 14. Causes of respiratory alkalosis include tissue hypoxia (e.g., pneumonia, aspiration, pulmonary embolism, bronchospasm, drowning, anemia, high altitude, cyanotic heart disease, circulatory failure), stimulation of chest receptors (e.g., pneumonia, asthma, pneumothorax, cardiac failure, pulmonary edema, respiratory distress syndrome, interstitial lung disease), and central respiratory drive stimulators (e.g., pain, anxiety, fever, high altitude, anemia, certain drugs, CNS disorders, caffeine overdose, progesterone). 15. Systemic diseases such as sepsis, liver failure, hyperthyroidism, pregnancy, iatrogenic causes during mechanical ventilation, carbon monoxide poisoning, recovery from metabolic acidosis, and heat exposure can also lead to respiratory alkalosis. 16. Special considerations include conditions like sepsis or salicylate toxicity, which can cause both elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis. CNS ischemia, infection, or infarction may result in either respiratory acidosis or alkalosis. Asthma and pneumonia can present with either respiratory alkalosis or acidosis, depending on the stage of the disease. Pulmonary embolism often presents as respiratory alkalosis. Progesterone is sometimes used as a respiratory stimulant in obstructive sleep apnea and hypoventilation. Respiratory alkalosis is the most common acid-base abnormality in critically ill patients. 17. Symptoms of respiratory alkalosis depend on the duration and underlying causes. Acute respiratory alkalosis symptoms are related to reduced blood CO2 levels (PaCO2), leading to decreased cerebral blood flow due to cerebral vasoconstriction. Symptoms typically arise when PaCO2 falls below 30 mmHg. Common symptoms include light-headedness, syncope, confusion, seizures, paresthesia, cramps, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Chronic respiratory alkalosis is generally well-tolerated without apparent symptoms. 18. Physical examination findings depend on the underlying cause. Patients with acute respiratory alkalosis may appear anxious in cases of primary hyperventilation syndrome or ill in mechanically ventilated cases, while those with chronic respiratory alkalosis appear comfortable. Vital signs may show fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, or hyperpnea. Cheyne-Stokes breathing may occur in upper pontine lesions or heart failure. Cyanosis may be present in hypoxic patients, and jaundice may be seen in liver disease. Neuromuscular findings include tetany and positive Trousseau sign in acute hypocapnia. 19. Diagnostic tests for respiratory alkalosis include arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis, serum electrolytes, urine pH, complete blood count (CBC), blood/sputum/urine cultures, ECG, echocardiography, drug screening, thyroid and liver function tests, pulmonary function tests, V/Q scan, chest X-ray, CT scan, and MRI brain imaging. 20. Treatment of respiratory alkalosis focuses on addressing the underlying cause. For hyperventilation disorders (e.g., anxiety, conversion disorder), rebreathing masks may be beneficial. High-altitude sickness is treated with acetazolamide, dexamethasone, oxygen therapy, and descent to lower altitudes in severe cases. For critically ill patients on mechanical ventilation, tidal volume and respiratory rate should be reduced with adequate pain control. Sedatives and antidepressants should not be used in respiratory alkalosis cases.
